claims.text: High-throughput computational screening combined with controlled annealing can be used to stabilize desired phases, refine microstructure, and optimize high-temperature mechanical properties in high-entropy alloys.
The optimization operates by tailoring the formation of load-bearing nanoscale precipitates.
The relevant material can be a multiphase Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti high-entropy alloy.
Slight compositional deviations determine whether the alloy forms nanoscale ordered precipitates or antiphase domains.
High-throughput screening can predict compositions and annealing parameters that favor finely dispersed ordered L21 precipitates.
Arc melting, homogenization, and annealing can be used experimentally after computational screening.
A high-temperature homogenization treatment at approximately 1200 °C is applicable to the screened Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti alloys.
A controlled anneal at approximately 700 °C for 2 hours is applicable to the screened alloys.
The relevant compositional range has Al below 25 at.% and Mn above 15 at.%.
The structural mediator is the morphology and distribution of an L21-ordered phase in a BCC matrix.
Computationally selected processing parameters alter the thermodynamic driving force for ordering.
Changing the thermodynamic driving force controls precipitate size, coherency, and volume fraction.
Fine, load-bearing precipitates improve load transfer and precipitation strengthening relative to coarser or less coherent phases.
The optimized alloy will contain a well-defined nanoscale distribution of L21 precipitates.
The optimized alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength than alloys processed without computationally targeted intervention.
Processing without computational guidance tends to produce dominant antiphase domains or coarser precipitates.
The uncontrolled baseline microstructure produces lower high-temperature yield strength.
The approach is most effective within a limited compositional window.
Prediction accuracy and resulting property improvements depend on the reliability of thermodynamic databases and on whether the models capture kinetic and compositional complexities.
